title: Introduction to WHOIS
shortDescription: Learn what WHOIS is and why it is important.
content: WHOIS is a protocol and database that provides registration information about domain names. Cybersecurity professionals use WHOIS to identify domain ownership, registrar information, creation dates, expiration dates and contact information when available.
example: Run 'whois example.com' to retrieve registration information.

title: Installing WHOIS
shortDescription: Learn how to install WHOIS on different operating systems.
content: WHOIS is preinstalled on many Linux distributions. Windows users can install WHOIS clients or use online services. macOS users can install it using Homebrew if necessary.
example: whois google.com

title: Running WHOIS Commands
content: The basic syntax is 'whois domain.com'. The output includes registrar details, registration dates, DNS servers and other registration information.
example: whois openai.com

title: Understanding WHOIS Output
content: WHOIS output contains registrar information, creation date, expiration date, updated date, domain status and name servers. Each field helps investigators gather intelligence about the target domain.
example: Identify the registrar of github.com using WHOIS.

title: WHOIS Best Practices
content: Always verify WHOIS results with multiple sources. Respect privacy regulations and remember that WHOIS information may be hidden due to privacy protection services.
example: Compare WHOIS information with DNS Lookup results.

title: Introduction to DNS Lookup
shortDescription: Learn how DNS records help in OSINT.
content: DNS translates domain names into network information. DNS Lookup can reveal records such as A, MX, NS, TXT and CNAME records.
example: Use nslookup example.com to view DNS information.

title: Basic DNS Queries
content: The nslookup utility can be used on Windows and other operating systems. Queries can retrieve different types of DNS records.
example: nslookup -type=MX example.com

title: Using DNS Results in Investigation
content: DNS information can help investigators understand domain infrastructure. Results should be correlated with WHOIS and other reconnaissance findings.
example: Compare DNS name servers with WHOIS name server information.

title: Introduction to theHarvester
shortDescription: Learn how theHarvester collects public reconnaissance information.
content: theHarvester is an OSINT reconnaissance tool that can collect publicly available email addresses, hosts and subdomains from supported sources.
example: Use theHarvester to research publicly available information about an authorized domain.

title: Installing and Running theHarvester
content: TheHarvester can be installed using supported Python distributions. A basic search specifies a domain and a data source.
example: theHarvester -d example.com -b bing

title: Analyzing theHarvester Results
content: TheHarvester results should be treated as leads. Investigators can compare discovered hosts and email addresses with DNS and other public sources.
example: Compare discovered subdomains with DNS Lookup results.

title: Introduction to Sherlock
content: Sherlock searches many websites to determine whether a username appears to exist on supported services.
example: Investigate an authorized test username.

title: Running Sherlock
content: Sherlock accepts a username as input and checks supported websites. Installation and execution should follow the official project documentation.
example: sherlock example_username

title: Analyzing Username Results
shortDescription: Learn how to validate Sherlock findings.
content: A matching username does not prove that accounts belong to the same person. Investigators should compare additional public indicators before drawing conclusions.
example: Compare profile information before linking two usernames.

title: Introduction to VirusTotal
shortDescription: Learn how VirusTotal supports threat intelligence.
content: VirusTotal aggregates security information from multiple security vendors and intelligence sources for files, URLs, domains and IP addresses.
example: Search a known safe test domain in VirusTotal.

title: Performing a VirusTotal Search
shortDescription: Learn how to investigate public indicators.
content: VirusTotal allows users to search supported indicators and review available detections, relationships and reputation information.
example: Search a public domain and review its available information.

title: Interpreting VirusTotal Results
content: A detection is an indicator for investigation rather than automatic proof of malicious activity. Results should be correlated with additional evidence.
example: Compare VirusTotal results with URLScan or other intelligence.

title: Introduction to nslookup
content: nslookup is a command-line DNS query utility available on Windows and other operating systems.
example: nslookup example.com

title: Basic nslookup Commands
content: nslookup can query common DNS record types such as A, MX and NS records.
example: nslookup -type=NS example.com

title: Analyzing nslookup Output
content: The response provides DNS server information and records returned for the query. Findings can be correlated with other domain information.
example: Identify the IP address returned for example.com.

title: Introduction to dig
shortDescription: Learn detailed DNS investigation with dig.
content: dig is a command-line utility that provides detailed DNS query and response information.
example: dig example.com

title: Running dig Queries
content: dig supports queries for many DNS record types and provides detailed response sections.
example: dig example.com MX

title: Understanding dig Output
content: Important parts of dig output include the question section, answer section, authority information and query statistics.
example: Use dig to compare DNS records for a test domain.

title: Introduction to DNSRecon
content: DNSRecon automates several DNS reconnaissance tasks and can help investigators collect domain DNS information.
example: Use DNSRecon on an authorized test domain.

title: Basic DNSRecon Usage
content: DNSRecon accepts a target domain and performs supported DNS enumeration tasks.
example: dnsrecon -d example.com

title: Analyzing DNSRecon Results
content: DNSRecon output can contain records and discovered infrastructure information. Results should be validated using independent DNS sources.
example: Compare DNSRecon results with dig.

title: Introduction to DNSenum
content: DNSenum is a DNS enumeration utility used to gather information about domains and their DNS infrastructure.
example: Use DNSenum only against an authorized test domain.

title: Running DNSenum
content: DNSenum can be executed with a target domain and produces DNS-related reconnaissance information.
example: dnsenum example.com

title: DNSenum Result Analysis
content: DNSenum findings should be compared with DNSRecon, dig or nslookup to identify consistent information.
example: Compare DNSenum and nslookup results.

title: Introduction to Fierce
content: Fierce is a DNS reconnaissance tool that can help identify hosts and DNS-related information associated with a domain.
example: Research an authorized domain using Fierce.

title: Basic Fierce Usage
content: Fierce accepts a domain as its primary input and performs DNS reconnaissance against that domain.
example: fierce --domain example.com

title: Analyzing Fierce Results
content: Discovered hosts should be validated through additional DNS and web sources before being treated as confirmed assets.
example: Compare discovered hosts with Subfinder results.

title: Introduction to Subfinder
content: Subfinder is designed for passive subdomain discovery using supported public sources.
example: subfinder -d example.com

title: Running Subfinder
content: Subfinder accepts a domain and queries supported passive sources to identify possible subdomains.
example: subfinder -d example.com

title: Analyzing Subfinder Results
content: Subdomain results are useful as investigation leads. Investigators should verify whether discovered hosts are active and relevant.
example: Compare Subfinder results with certificate transparency records.

title: Introduction to Amass
content: Amass is an open-source tool for network mapping and asset discovery, including domain and subdomain enumeration.
example: Use passive enumeration on an authorized domain.

title: Basic Amass Usage
content: Amass provides several enumeration modes. Passive enumeration can collect information from public sources without directly probing the target.
example: amass enum -passive -d example.com

title: Analyzing Amass Results
content: Amass can produce many findings. Investigators should organize discovered domains and correlate them with DNS, certificates and other sources.
example: Compare Amass results with Subfinder.

title: Introduction to Assetfinder
content: Assetfinder is a lightweight tool for finding domains and subdomains related to a target.
example: assetfinder example.com

title: Running Assetfinder
content: Assetfinder accepts a domain and searches supported sources for related assets.
example: assetfinder example.com

title: Validating Assetfinder Results
content: Discovered domains should be compared with DNS and other reconnaissance sources before being considered confirmed assets.
example: Compare Assetfinder results with Subfinder.

title: Introduction to Maigret
content: Maigret searches many websites for a specified username and can provide useful leads for online identity investigations.
example: maigret example_username

title: Running Maigret
content: Maigret takes a username as input and checks supported websites for possible matches.
example: maigret example_username

title: Analyzing Maigret Results
shortDescription: Learn how to validate username matches.
content: Username matches are only leads. Investigators should compare profile information and other public indicators before linking accounts.
example: Compare two matching profiles using public profile information.

title: Introduction to WhatsMyName
content: WhatsMyName is a public username investigation resource that helps identify possible accounts across online services.
example: Search an authorized test username.

title: Performing Username Searches
content: A username can be checked against supported websites. The results should be manually reviewed for relevance.
example: Search a test username across supported services.

title: Validating Username Findings
content: A shared username does not establish that two accounts belong to one individual. Additional public evidence is required.
example: Compare usernames with profile biography and public links.

title: Introduction to Holehe
content: Holehe checks supported online services for indicators that an email address may be registered.
example: Use a test email address in a controlled lab.

title: Running Holehe
content: Holehe accepts an email address and performs checks against supported services. Use only addresses you are authorized to investigate.
example: holehe test@example.com

title: Analyzing Holehe Results
content: Results indicate possible service registration and should not automatically be treated as proof of account ownership.
example: Record possible matches and validate them using authorized evidence.

title: Introduction to PhoneInfoga
content: PhoneInfoga is an OSINT tool designed to gather publicly available information about phone numbers.
example: Use a test number in a controlled investigation.

title: Running PhoneInfoga
content: PhoneInfoga supports phone number reconnaissance. Investigators should only use numbers they are authorized to investigate.
example: phoneinfoga scan -n +1234567890

title: Interpreting Phone OSINT Results
shortDescription: Learn to validate phone investigation findings.
content: Phone OSINT results can provide useful leads but may be incomplete or outdated. Important findings should be independently verified.
example: Cross-check available information using independent public sources.

title: Introduction to Google Dorking
content: Google Dorking uses advanced search operators to narrow publicly indexed information.
example: site:example.com filetype:pdf

title: Using Search Operators
content: Operators such as site:, filetype:, intitle: and inurl: can help focus searches on specific public content.
example: site:example.com filetype:pdf

title: Responsible Google Dorking
content: Search operators should be used for legitimate research and security education. Finding indexed information does not grant permission to access restricted resources.
example: Search publicly available documentation on an authorized domain.

title: Introduction to Google Lens
content: Google Lens provides visual search capabilities that can help investigators locate visually similar images and public information.
example: Use a public test image for visual search.

title: Performing a Visual Search
shortDescription: Learn how to search using images.
content: An image can be submitted to Google Lens to identify visually similar images, objects or related public information.
example: Upload a non-sensitive sample image and inspect the results.

title: Analyzing Image Search Results
content: Visual similarity does not prove that two images are the same event or source. Investigators should verify dates, context and original sources.
example: Compare a sample image with its public search results.

title: Introduction to ExifTool
content: ExifTool is a powerful utility for reading metadata from images and many other file formats.
example: exiftool image.jpg

title: Extracting Metadata
content: ExifTool can display metadata such as camera information, timestamps, file properties and location information when present.
example: exiftool image.jpg

title: Analyzing Metadata
content: Metadata can provide useful investigation clues, but it may be modified or removed. Important findings should be validated.
example: Compare image metadata with the image's public context.

title: Introduction to WhatWeb
content: WhatWeb identifies technologies and components used by websites through fingerprinting techniques.
example: whatweb example.com

title: Running WhatWeb
content: WhatWeb accepts a website target and attempts to identify technologies such as web servers, frameworks and applications.
example: whatweb example.com

title: Analyzing WhatWeb Results
content: Technology fingerprints are indicators rather than absolute proof. Important findings should be confirmed using additional evidence.
example: Compare WhatWeb findings with another technology detection source.

title: Introduction to Wappalyzer
content: Wappalyzer identifies technologies used by websites, including frameworks, analytics platforms and web services.
example: Open a public website with Wappalyzer.

title: Using Wappalyzer
shortDescription: Learn how to inspect website technologies.
content: Wappalyzer can be used through supported browser extensions or services to inspect publicly observable website technologies.
example: Inspect a test website and record detected technologies.

title: Comparing Technology Findings
content: Technology detection can vary between tools. Comparing Wappalyzer results with WhatWeb can improve confidence.
example: Compare Wappalyzer and WhatWeb results for a public test website.

title: Introduction to Nmap
content: Nmap is a network discovery and security auditing tool. It can identify hosts and services on authorized networks.
example: Use Nmap only against systems you are authorized to assess.

title: Basic Nmap Scanning
content: Nmap can identify reachable services and ports. Active scanning should only be performed against authorized targets.
example: nmap example.com

title: Understanding Nmap Results
content: Nmap results commonly identify port states and services. Findings can be recorded as part of an authorized investigation.
example: Review the ports reported for a lab machine.

title: Introduction to Shodan
content: Shodan is a search engine for internet-connected devices and services and can provide passive infrastructure intelligence.
example: Search for a public domain you are authorized to research.

title: Searching Shodan
content: Shodan supports searches for internet-facing hosts, services and other indexed information.
example: Search Shodan for a test domain or known public IP.

title: Analyzing Shodan Results
content: Shodan data can help build an external attack-surface picture. Results should be checked for freshness and relevance.
example: Compare Shodan information with DNS findings.

title: Introduction to Censys
shortDescription: Learn internet host and certificate intelligence.
content: Censys provides searchable information about internet hosts, services and certificates.
example: Search a public test domain in Censys.

title: Searching Censys
content: Censys can be used to investigate publicly observable hosts and certificate information associated with internet infrastructure.
example: Search certificate information for a public domain.

title: Analyzing Censys Findings
content: Certificate and host information can reveal relationships between domains and infrastructure. Findings should be validated.
example: Compare Censys certificate information with crt.sh.

title: Introduction to crt.sh
content: crt.sh provides a searchable interface for public Certificate Transparency records.
example: Search for certificates associated with a test domain.

title: Finding Domains in Certificates
content: Certificate records can contain domain names and subdomains that help investigators understand an organization's public infrastructure.
example: Search %.example.com in crt.sh.

title: Analyzing Certificate Findings
content: Certificate records indicate that names appeared in certificates, but they do not necessarily prove that the corresponding hosts are currently active.
example: Compare crt.sh results with current DNS records.

title: Introduction to SecurityTrails
content: SecurityTrails provides domain and DNS intelligence that can help investigators understand current and historical infrastructure.
example: Research a public domain using SecurityTrails.

title: Searching Domain Information
content: SecurityTrails can provide information about DNS records and domain infrastructure depending on available access.
example: Search a test domain and inspect available DNS history.

title: Using Historical DNS Data
shortDescription: Learn how historical data supports investigations.
content: Historical DNS information can help investigators understand changes in infrastructure over time.
example: Compare historical DNS information with current DNS records.

title: Introduction to URLScan.io
content: URLScan.io provides public website scan information including page, network and domain-related details.
example: Search a public website scan.

title: Analyzing a URL
content: URLScan.io can provide information about page resources, domains, requests and other publicly observable characteristics.
example: Search for a public URL scan.

title: Interpreting URLScan Results
content: URLScan results can help investigators understand relationships between webpages, domains and external resources.
example: Compare URLScan domains with DNS findings.

title: Introduction to Have I Been Pwned
content: Have I Been Pwned provides a way to check whether an email address appears in known data breaches.
example: Check an authorized email address.

title: Checking an Email Address
content: Users can search an email address through the service to determine whether it appears in known breach datasets.
example: Check a test email address.

title: Understanding Breach Results
shortDescription: Learn how to interpret breach information.
content: A breach result indicates that an identifier appeared in a known dataset. It does not necessarily indicate current account compromise.
example: Record the breach name and date when documenting an authorized investigation.

title: Introduction to Wayback Machine
content: The Wayback Machine stores historical snapshots of many publicly accessible websites.
example: Search a public domain for archived pages.

title: Finding Historical Pages
shortDescription: Learn how to navigate archived websites.
content: Users can select archived dates and inspect available historical versions of websites.
example: Compare a website's current page with an older snapshot.

title: Using Archived Evidence
content: Archived pages can provide historical context. Investigators should record the snapshot date and distinguish archived information from current information.
example: Record the date of an archived page used in an investigation.

title: Introduction to SpiderFoot
content: SpiderFoot is an OSINT automation platform that can gather information from many supported sources.
example: Use SpiderFoot in an authorized lab environment.

title: Running an OSINT Scan
content: SpiderFoot can be configured to investigate domains, IP addresses and other supported targets using selected modules.
example: Create a scan for an authorized lab domain.

title: Analyzing SpiderFoot Results
shortDescription: Learn how to organize automated OSINT findings.
content: Automated OSINT can generate a large amount of information. Investigators should organize, validate and correlate important findings.
example: Group domain, email and infrastructure findings into an investigation.

title: Introduction to Hunter.io
content: Hunter.io provides email intelligence and domain-related information useful for legitimate business OSINT research.
example: Research a public business domain.

title: Searching Domain Email Information
content: Hunter.io can provide publicly available email-related information associated with domains, subject to service limits.
example: Search a public test domain.

title: Analyzing Email Intelligence
content: Email intelligence should be treated as a lead. Important information should be confirmed through additional legitimate sources.
example: Compare Hunter results with public company information.

title: Introduction to Google for OSINT
shortDescription: Learn web search as an OSINT technique.
content: Google can be used to locate publicly available information across the indexed web.
example: Search for publicly available information about a test domain.

title: Effective Google Searching
content: Good OSINT searches use precise keywords and appropriate search operators to reduce irrelevant results.
example: Search for official documentation related to a domain.

title: Validating Google Findings
content: Search results should be treated as discovery aids. Important claims should be verified using reliable primary or authoritative sources.
example: Verify information using an organization's official website.

title: Introduction to Bing for OSINT
content: Bing is a search engine that can provide an alternative index for public web research.
example: Search a public test domain.

title: Performing Bing Searches
content: Bing supports search queries and operators that can help refine publicly available information.
example: Search for public PDF documents related to a topic.

title: Comparing Search Results
shortDescription: Use Bing as a second search source.
content: Different search engines may index different pages. Comparing results can improve the coverage of an OSINT investigation.
example: Compare a query's Google and Bing results.

title: Introduction to DuckDuckGo
content: DuckDuckGo is a privacy-focused search engine that can be used as an additional source for public web research.
example: Search a public topic using DuckDuckGo.

title: Performing DuckDuckGo Searches
content: Precise keywords and supported operators can help investigators locate relevant public information.
example: Search for public documentation about a domain.

title: Using Multiple Search Engines
content: Using multiple search engines can reveal different indexed pages and improve the completeness of an investigation.
example: Compare the same query across Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo.

title: Introduction to Yandex
shortDescription: Learn alternative web and visual search.
content: Yandex is a search engine that can provide alternative web and image search results useful for OSINT research.
example: Search a public topic using Yandex.

title: Searching with Yandex
content: Yandex can be used to search public web and visual information. Search results can differ from other engines.
example: Search for public images related to a test subject.

title: Comparing Yandex Results
content: Alternative search indexes can provide additional leads. Important information should still be verified using reliable sources.
example: Compare image results from Yandex and Google Lens.

title: Introduction to Brave Search
content: Brave Search is a privacy-oriented search engine that can provide another source for public web research.
example: Search a public research topic.

title: Performing Brave Searches
content: Use precise keywords and supported search features to find relevant public information.
example: Search for public information about an authorized domain.

title: Cross-Checking Search Results
content: Search engines can return different results. Comparing sources helps identify useful leads and reduce dependence on one index.
example: Compare Brave Search results with Google.

title: Introduction to Mojeek
content: Mojeek is an independent search engine that can provide alternative public web results.
example: Search a public research topic.

title: Performing Mojeek Searches
content: Use relevant keywords and search features to locate public information.
example: Search for public documentation.

title: Using Mojeek in OSINT
content: Mojeek can be used alongside other search engines to increase discovery coverage during OSINT research.
example: Compare Mojeek results with Google and Bing.
